analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to cover cheaper generics and biosimilars with lower copays.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill would force Medicare drug plans to put cheaper generics and biosimilars on their formularies with copays at least $20 below brand-drug tiers, but so far it has gone no further than referral to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require Medicare Part D drug plans that use formularies to include any generic drug priced below its brand-name counterpart, and at least one cheaper biosimilar for any brand biologic on the formulary. Plans could not make those cheaper drugs harder to get than the brand versions through prior authorization or step therapy, and would have to put them on a low-cost tier with a copay at least $20 below the cheapest brand tier. The rules would not take effect until plan year 2028.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, particularly seniors who take brand-name drugs or biologics with generic or biosimilar competitors, would get guaranteed access to the cheaper version with fewer coverage hurdles and lower copays. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers would gain guaranteed formulary placement and favorable cost-sharing tiers that increase their sales.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare who use generics

how_it_helps.text: Requires Part D plans to include on their formularies every generic drug whose list price is below the brand-name reference drug on the formulary, and at least one biosimilar priced below any reference biologic on the formulary.

Bars plans from imposing prior authorization, utilization management, or step therapy on those generics and biosimilars that is stricter than what the brand versions face, and from giving the brand preferred status over the cheaper version.
Requires plans with tiered cost-sharing to create a tier containing only generics and biosimilars, with either no copay or a copay at least $20 lower than the lowest branded tier.
Requires plans with a specialty tier to add a second specialty tier for high-cost generics and biosimilars with coinsurance at least 5 percentage points lower than other specialty tiers.
Stops plans from applying a deductible only to generics and biosimilars while waiving it for other drugs, so cheaper drugs cannot be pushed behind a deductible the brand avoids.

analysis.who_pays: Part D prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers bear the cost: they lose flexibility to steer patients toward drugs with the best rebate deals, must guarantee placement and low cost-sharing for generics and biosimilars, and may pass some of that through in premiums. Brand-name drug and biologic manufacturers lose the preferred formulary positioning that protects their sales from cheaper competitors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Part D insurers and brand drugmakers

drawbacks.text: The requirement is triggered by wholesale acquisition cost — the drug's published list price — not the net price after rebates and discounts, so a brand drug with heavy rebates could actually cost a plan less than the generic the bill forces onto the formulary.
Nothing changes until plan year 2028, so beneficiaries get no relief in the near term even if the bill passed quickly.

By mandating formulary inclusion and tier placement, the bill reduces plan flexibility and adds compliance costs, which insurers would tend to recover through higher premiums; the bill also prevents plans from offering zero or reduced deductibles for generics alone unless extended more broadly, taking away one tool plans use to make cheap drugs attractive.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: seniors would be guaranteed access to the cheaper version of a drug they need, without extra paperwork hurdles, at a copay meaningfully below the brand tier. The main design flaw is that the trigger uses list price rather than net price after rebates, which could force coverage of generics that are not genuinely cheaper for the plan; the 2028 effective date also delays any benefit. The costs fall on insurers and brand manufacturers rather than directly on patients, though some could surface in premiums.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee, where it sits with no further action while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Lankford introduced the bill on April 16, 2026, joined by Senator Hassan and one other Democratic cosponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote has followed.
Congress remains in session until January 3, 2027, so the bill could still move, but it has not advanced past the referral stage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, Part D insurers and brand-name drug makers, who keep their current formulary control and preferred positioning because the bill has not advanced; seniors gain nothing until and unless it moves.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and brand drugmakers, for now

for.name: Sen. James Lankford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it.

for.name: Sen. Maggie Hassan
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; the bill was introduced for Lankford and Hassan together.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Holds the bill; it has taken no action since the April 16, 2026 referral.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator introduced the bill with two Democratic cosponsors, and no votes have occurred to reveal a partisan split.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers (prescription drug plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers)
industries.note: The bill strips plans of control over whether cheap generics and biosimilars make it onto formularies and how hard they are to access, and dictates their cost-sharing tiers. Their savings from steering patients to rebate-rich brands shrink, and costs could flow into premiums.

Brands and biologics lose the ability to keep cheaper competitors off formularies or behind extra hoops. Where a generic or biosimilar exists, the bill forces plans to cover it and forbids preferring the brand over it.
Guaranteed formulary placement, protection from stricter utilization management, and dedicated low-cost tiers would increase demand for their products.

The formulary design and rebate-steering tools PBMs use on behalf of plans — prior authorization, step therapy, tier placement — are curtailed exactly where generics and biosimilars compete with brands.

analysis.trajectory: The bill must clear the Senate Finance Committee and then win floor time in a chamber that moved it only to referral in its first eight months. Standalone Medicare formulary bills at this stage rarely get their own vote; the realistic path is attachment to a larger health or Medicare package, which is possible but not likely before the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
